title: MemLeak: Cross-User Semantic Leakage in Multi-Tenant AI Agent Memory

object.carrier: Pooled multi-tenant long-term memory: a single shared vector store (e.g., Mem0/A-Mem/MemOS pattern) holding per-user memories as embeddings with soft user_id metadata rather than a hard-enforced boundary; top-k cosine-similarity retrieval injects memories into the agent LLM context

safety_property.statement: In a multi-tenant agent deployment with pooled/scoped memory, one user's private long-term memories must not be admitted into another user's agent session; the property fails when a memory owned by another user ranks in top-k by cosine similarity (cross-user admissibility failure), judged by leakage rate, attacker top-k placement, and downstream response contamination. It holds under strict per-user partitioning (ACL baseline, LR 0%).
safety_property.operationalized_as: LR = fraction of queries with >=1 cross-user memory in top-k; top-k placement rate for crafted attacker memories; judge-rated contamination score (1-5) with clean baseline 1.00; all rates over n=10 queries per condition with 95% Wilson CIs (metric definitions in Appendix B Table 9).

capabilities: Passive scenario: ordinary users interact normally; cross-user retrieval happens organically with no adversarial intent
Active scenario (Mallory): crafts and writes ordinary professional memories into a shared or in-scope store designed to rank highly for the victim's expected queries
Mallory knows the victim's general domain and role (e.g., budget approvals) but not exact queries or embedding-model internals, and has no oracle access to the input stream
No exploit beyond ordinary usage: no prompt injection, no code change, no model-weight modification, no explicit data transfer
assumptions: Memories of many users co-exist in a pooled vector index where ownership exists only as soft metadata filtering (or in intentionally widened team/project/scoped-workflow scopes)
Retrieval ranks candidates purely by cosine similarity and injects top-k into the LLM context
An attacker may be a malicious or compromised in-scope member (team/project/role scope)
not_covered: Strict per-user partitioned indices are out of scope (treated as the ACL baseline and confirmed to give 0% leakage)
Prompt injection, corpus poisoning with adversarial instructions, and model-weight attacks (retrieved memories are ordinary notes)
Functioning covert channel: E6's sequential multi-bit transmission fails (negative result); capacity measurement left to future work
LLM-based (non-embedding) memory selection not evaluated empirically
User-conditioned encoder training for M2 beyond proof-of-concept proxies

intervention.name: M3: hard post-retrieval ownership gating
intervention.description: After pooled cosine retrieval, drop retrieved hits whose owner differs from the querying user (hard gate), contrasted with a suspicion gate that drops cross-user hits exceeding a similarity threshold. Hard gating eliminates crafted-memory placement (0%) and restores mean downstream contamination to the clean baseline 1.00/5 for both generation models and both memory paths at ~1.4 ms mean latency per query (1,000 cycles, 10k-memory pgvector HNSW). M1 metadata filtering succeeds only under partitioning and fails once the attacker falls inside a widened scope (scoped_cross restores 90-100% placement); M2 prefix injection partially reduces T0 leakage (70% to 50%) while raising same-user utility (0.384 to 0.506), and the namespace-offset variant backfires.

results.claim: Under pooled same-team retrieval, incidental cross-user leakage is systematic in both configurations (100% sparse TF-IDF, 70% dense MiniLM) in the paper's synthetic fixtures.
results.setting: T0 same-team pair (Alice/Bob), 10 memories and 10 managerial queries, hand-authored fixtures, top-k=3 cosine retrieval, n=10 queries per condition
results.quote: Config A exhibits 100% LR with a larger score gap (+0.244+0.244), consistent with sparse TF-IDF increasing lexical overlap. Config B reduces incidental leakage to 70% while maintaining mean cross-user rank below 2.0

denominator.how_counted: Table 1 caption: LR = leakage rate over n=10 queries, with 95% Wilson-score CI; Table 9: LR = fraction of queries with >=1 cross-user memory in top-k

results.claim: User-scoped partitioned retrieval eliminates incidental leakage entirely (the ACL baseline), with no cross-user hits observed in either configuration.
results.setting: Same T0 fixtures as E1, partitioned (user-scoped) index mode for both TF-IDF and MiniLM configurations
results.quote: Under partitioned retrieval, LR =0%=0\% in both configurations with no cross-user hits observed, confirming that user-scoped indexing eliminates incidental leakage in our fixtures; this partitioned condition is the ACL baseline described in Section 3.5.

denominator.how_counted: Table 1 caption: LR = leakage rate over n=10 queries, with 95% Wilson-score CI

results.claim: The cross-company control (T3) is the only clearly separated tier at 10% leakage under Config B, while pooled in-organization tiers T0-T2 reach 70-100%; organizational distance is not a reliable fine-grained risk proxy.
results.setting: Four synthetic user pairs at organizational distances T0-T3, Config B MiniLM pooled retrieval, n=10 queries per condition
results.quote: The cross-company control (T3) drops to 10% LR under Config B (95% CI [2%, 40%]) with mean cross-user rank 3.00, a robust contrast with pooled retrieval generally (70–100% across T0–T2; Table 4).

denominator.how_counted: Table 3 caption: E2 leakage rate (LR, with 95% Wilson CI, n=10)

results.claim: Adversarially crafted memories achieve 90-100% top-k placement in both configurations, far above organic placement, without any exploit.
results.comparison: organic placement as low as 10% (Config B Salary), 0% in some scenarios, up to 70% (Config A Budget)
results.setting: Three scenarios (Salary Negotiation, Security Policy, Budget Authority), attacker Mallory writes crafted bridging memories, TF-IDF and MiniLM pooled retrieval, top-k=3, n=10 queries
results.quote: Crafted memories achieve 90–100% top-kk placement in both configurations, compared with organic placement as low as 10% (Salary Negotiation, Config B; Table 2), reaching 0% in some scenarios (full grid in Appendix F), and as high as 70% (Budget Authority, Config A).

denominator.how_counted: Table 2 caption: Pl.% = top-k placement rate for crafted memories; Table 9: Fraction with attacker memory in top-k

results.claim: Placement rises monotonically with assumed attacker knowledge, and crafted bridging assuming only domain/role knowledge closes most of the gap to the verbatim-copy oracle.
results.comparison: 10% organic -> 40% keyword bag -> 80% per-query keywords -> 90% crafted -> 100% verbatim oracle
results.setting: Salary Negotiation scenario, Config B MiniLM, k=3, attacker-knowledge baselines of increasing query knowledge, 95% Wilson CIs
results.quote: Under Config B, placement rises monotonically with assumed attacker knowledge: 10% (organic) →\to 40% (domain keyword bag) →\to 80% (per-query keywords) →\to 90% (crafted bridging, ours) →\to 100% (verbatim-copy oracle)

denominator.how_counted: Section 4.1: each rate computed over n=10 queries per condition; Appendix F Table 10 with 95% Wilson CIs

results.claim: Leaked memories measurably contaminate downstream responses, with the end-to-end retrieval path and Gemini 2.5 Flash reaching the maximum 5.00/5 contamination while responses stay helpful.
results.setting: E4 mean over 3 scenarios; static vs full retrieve-then-generate paths (Config B); Gemini 2.5 Flash and Claude Sonnet 4.5 as generator and self-judge at temperature 0; clean baseline = 1.00/5 in all conditions
results.quote: The retrieval path with Gemini 2.5 Flash yields maximum contamination (5.00/5, Δ=+4.00\Delta=+4.00), demonstrating that end-to-end retrieval increases downstream harm relative to static injection. Claude Sonnet 4.5 achieves 4.67/5 under both static and retrieval paths

results.claim: Hard post-retrieval ownership gating is the only mitigation that consistently eliminates crafted-memory placement and restores downstream contamination to the clean baseline for both generators and both memory paths.
results.metric: attacker top-k placement rate; E4 contamination score
results.value: 0% attacker placement; 1.00/5 mean contamination (= clean baseline)
results.setting: M3 under Config B on E3 active exploitation and E4 downstream contamination with Gemini 2.5 Flash and Claude Sonnet 4.5; ungated mean placement was 97% (Table 7)
results.quote: Hard ownership gating eliminates Mallory placement in E3 (0%; Table 7) and reduces mean E4 contamination to 1.00/5, which is the clean baseline for both generation models and both memory paths (Table 8)

denominator.how_counted: Table 7: crafted-memory top-k placement rate per scenario and mean; Table 8: mean E4 contamination scores over 3 scenarios

results.claim: The recommended hard ownership gate is deployable at negligible measured cost, adding roughly 1.4 ms of mean latency per query in a realistic serving path.
results.setting: 1,000 query cycles against a 10,000-memory pgvector HNSW index with over-fetch K=15; unfiltered baseline 12.4 ms (Appendix J Table 14)
results.quote: Applying deterministic post-retrieval ownership gating (M3) adds roughly 1.4 ms of mean latency per query while eliminating measured response contamination, indicating the mitigation is deployable at negligible cost in a realistic serving path.

limitations.statement: All results come from a small controlled proof-of-concept design (4 hand-authored user pairs, n=10 queries per condition), so fine-grained orderings are only suggestive and rates are not population-level prevalence estimates.
limitations.quote: Our results rest on a controlled proof-of-concept design: four hand-authored synthetic user pairs and n=10n=10 queries per condition (three scenarios for downstream contamination), so fine-grained rank orderings between conditions with overlapping 95% Wilson intervals (e.g., T1/T2 vs. T0 in E2, or the Resonance Index ordering in E5) should be read as suggestive rather than established, and our rates are not a population-level prevalence estimate for real enterprise deployments.

limitations.statement: Memories and queries are synthetic hand-authored fixtures, not samples from production data, and their representativeness is unverified.
limitations.quote: Memories and queries are fixed, hand-authored fixtures rather than samples from production logs, and we have not verified their representativeness.

limitations.statement: E4/M3 contamination is self-judged by the same model family as the generator; a small human-agreement pilot (n=9) was weaker on contamination, and the numbers are treated as a conservative lower bound.
limitations.quote: Downstream contamination and helpfulness in E4/M3 are scored by the same model family used as generator; a small human-agreement pilot (n=9n=9, Section 4.7) found strong agreement on clean controls and helpfulness but weaker agreement on contamination, with the one disagreement suggesting our reported numbers are a conservative lower bound rather than an inflated estimate.

limitations.statement: Only embedding-similarity retrieval and two generation/judge models are studied, and the mitigations are proof-of-concept implementations rather than production deployments.
limitations.quote: We study only embedding-similarity retrieval and evaluate two generation/judge models, and our mitigations are proof-of-concept implementations rather than production deployments.
